column3: Howlett's "the Temple was begun, 958 B.C." is held as an `alternate` claim on event:israel.monarchy.temple-begun under profile `catholic-traditional-v1`, while the two other figures from the identical source sentence (the 1277 B.C. Exodus and the 1020 B.C. accession of Saul) were withdrawn from the same profile as modern-critical chronology.
column4: artifact.catholic-encyclopedia.volume-3.new-york-1908.newadvent-03731a-f5f96f04 — James Howlett, "Biblical Chronology", The Catholic Encyclopedia vol. 3 (New York: Robert Appleton, 1908); src/sources/chronology/events.yaml; guidance/scripture-chronology.md §4.1, §4.2, §4.3, §4.4
column5: Howlett, "Biblical Chronology", the closing sentence of the section "The Exodus to the building of Solomon's Temple" (retained text via .scratch/cold-audit/src.py, section heading at line 173, the sentence at line 174)
column8: THE EXACT SENTENCE, reopened and read in the retained source: "We conclude, therefore, that the date of the Exodus was about 1277, the monarchy was founded by Saul, 1020; David mounted the throne, 1002; Solomon in 962, and the Temple was begun, 958 B.C." WHO ASSERTS IT: Howlett himself, in the article's own voice — "We conclude, therefore". He ADOPTS it; he does not report it as another's figure. WHAT IT RESTS ON: the whole of the preceding paragraph, which is a modern-critical argument and nothing else. Howlett opens "The Third Book of Kings (vi, 1) states that Solomon began to build the Temple in the 480th year ... For the Catholic, that passage seems to settle the question. But a difficulty arises from the fact that there is almost a consensus of scientific opinion that the Exodus from Egypt took place in the reign of Meneptah"; he cites "Assyriologists and Egyptologists agree" and Driver's "Genesis"; he takes Ramses II's reign "from 1348-1281 (Sayce)" and is "driven ... to about the year 1277 (Early History of the Hebrews, 150) for the date of the Exodus"; he concedes "we are left with only about 327 years, as against 480 required by 1 Kings 6:1"; and he closes the case by invoking the critics — "Wellhausen and Stade regard 6:1, as a late insertion (Burney, 'Hebrew Text of Kings', 58). If this were the case it would meet the difficulty". The 958 is the terminal figure of that chain and of nothing else: it is 962 minus the four regnal years, and 962 descends from the 1277. There is no independent traditional ground for 958 anywhere in the article. ADMISSIBILITY under `catholic-traditional-v1`: §4.1 — the profile "is not normalised to modern archaeological, Egyptological, Assyriological or critical-historical chronology", and "A modern chronology, if ever wanted, is a separate profile with its own id — never a silent correction of this one". §4.3 — "Modern critical chronology. Not consulted, not used to adjust a traditional date, not treated as a correction." §4.3 grants a reporting licence to Ussher BY NAME ("may be reported where a ranked Catholic source itself prints his figures") and pointedly grants none to modern critical chronology; that asymmetry is why claim #2 on this same event (Howlett PRINTING Ussher's 1010) is admissible and this one is not. §4.2 — "A lower rank is consulted only where every higher rank is silent": rank 1 is not silent here, it is the preferred claim on this very subject (3 Kings 6:1), and the 958 exists only by setting that verse aside. THE LANE'S OWN RULE, from its ledger for the twin figure E1-009: "Removing the claim, not re-disposing it, because Sec. 4.3's reporting licence is granted to Ussher alone ... and expressly NOT to modern critical chronology. An `alternate` would still be a modern figure consulted inside this profile." E2-004 asserts the opposite for the same figure from the same sentence — "admissible exactly because it is `alternate` beneath a preferred rank-1 claim" — and §4.4 supports no such route: §4.4 ranks claims already admitted, it does not admit a source class §4.3 excludes. E2-004's stated distinction is also not factually available: at 2330d63a5 event:israel.exodus.the-exodus held FOUR claims including the rank-1 3 Kings 6:1 interval, and the 1277 was removed anyway; it became possible to prefer Scripture there only BECAUSE the modern figure went. WHAT A CONSUMER GETS TODAY: `tools/tpt scripture-chronology query 3Kings.6.1` returns "narrated-event | the Temple was begun, 958 B.C. | alternate | direct | israel.monarchy.temple-begun", listed indistinguishably beside Petavius's 1012, Ussher-as-reported's 1010, Sloet's 969 and Meistermann's 966. The claim's note does say "Howlett's own reconstruction, not the traditional figure", and that disclosure is accurate and was rightly preserved — but the note is not in the default view, and a disclosure does not make an excluded source class admissible; the-exodus's 1277 carried the same disclosure and was still withdrawn. THE E2-004 PROSE EDIT ITSELF IS CORRECT and I verified it separately: the 958 closes "The Exodus to the building of Solomon's Temple" and the "about 969" closes "Building of the Temple to its destruction", which is the immediately following section, so "in the next section" is right and "four sections later" was wrong.
column9: Withdraw event:israel.monarchy.temple-begun#5 — the `alternate` carrying precision year, from {year: 958, era: bc}, label "the Temple was begun, 958 B.C." — from profile `catholic-traditional-v1` entirely, on exactly the ground and by exactly the method used for event:israel.exodus.the-exodus#1 under E1-009: remove the claim rather than re-dispose it, and record the figure and the profile boundary in the event's subject NOTE, which already names 958 among the figures the inspected articles print. Nothing structural breaks: the event retains a preferred rank-1 claim (3 Kings 6:1) and five other alternates, so §4.4's one-preferred rule and the loader's non-empty-dates rule are both still satisfied. The subject note should say, in the shape the-exodus's note already uses, that Howlett's own reckoning closes at 958 B.C. and is reached on Sayce's Egyptological dates and on Wellhausen's and Stade's treatment of 3 Kings 6:1 as a late insertion, and that it is recorded and not held because a modern chronology is a separate profile with its own id.
column10: CONSEQUENTIAL, FLAGGED NOT RULED — outside this package's row but found while reopening the source. event:israel.monarchy.temple-begun#4, Howlett's "the Temple was built about 969", stands on the same reconstruction: in the next section Howlett reaches it by "bringing to our help the fragment of the Tyrian annals quoted by Josephus, the foundation of the Temple may be fixed, according to Sayce, for about the year 969", inside a section whose stated project is that the chronology of the kings "must be made to accord with the Assyrian chronology". Whoever acts on RR-090 should rule on #4 in the same breath. Its case is weaker than #5's in one respect only: 969 has independent traditional support in the corpus from Sloet's table (#3, a different source and a different artifact), whereas 958 has none. I have NOT ruled on #3 or #4. Separately: the disposition STRUCTURE on this event is legal and is not the defect — one `preferred` (rank 1) with six rank-6 `alternate`s satisfies §4.4's "strictly higher authority rank than every alternate", and there is no `disputed`. The defect is admissibility under §4.1/§4.3, which is decided before disposition. Note also that the audit's earlier PASS on this claim (P-008) and the lane's E2-004 both examined the NOTE and the section count; neither reopened the sentence to ask what the "therefore" refers back to.

column8: BYTES: I fetched both URLs myself. g.htm -> sha256 064c6c3b4e1ff67f54711efd795ae465ca2100e58ce731d7a2fd7eb0203ef0ff, 32272 bytes; n.htm -> sha256 ef3ba0eb6967f4a243a94ffe21695eb3827d97223c8c42e6eeb0f7825b5454cd, 22935 bytes. Both match the registered sha256 and byte_size EXACTLY. `tools/tpt source-library validate` passes (artifact=1918 edition=722 work=540). ABSENCE, verified myself: g.htm's Gene- run is exactly "Genealogy (in the Bible)" (06408a), "Genealogy of Christ" (06410a), "General Judgment" (08552a), "Generation" (06412c), "Genesius" (06413c), "Genevieve, Saint" (06413f); the string "Genesis" occurs NOWHERE in the page. n.htm's Nu- run is "Nubia" (11147a), "Numbers, Use of, in the Church" (11151a), "Numismatics" (11152a), "Nun of Kent" (02319b); no entry for the book. THE DEFECT: both registered pages print, in their own words, above the first entry: "This list represents only a tiny fraction of articles available on the New Advent website. For a more complete list, please see the full index for G [N] or use the search box at the top of this page." The registered pages are New Advent's ABRIDGED letter indexes (162 and ~150 links). Against that, work.toml asserts of this work: "one page per initial letter, listing every article the encyclopedia carries under that letter ... a chronology gap row's evidence can be the ABSENCE of an entry from it", and each artifact record asserts "the encyclopedia carries no article on the biblical book in question, and only the index can establish that". That is refuted by the registered bytes themselves and, internally, by the Genesis gap row, which in the same sentence names "General Chapter" (06412b) and "Genesareth" (06413a) as real articles in that stretch - and neither appears in g.htm. The Numbers gap row goes further and is consumer-facing: `tools/tpt scripture-chronology query Num.11.1` prints "its FULL index for N carries only 'Numbers, Use of, in the Church' (11151a)", while the artifact it cites is n.htm, the abridged index, not the full one. I then fetched the real full indexes: g-ce.htm (546 links) lists under Gene- only "Genesareth" (06413a) and "Genesius" (06413c) and no Genesis; n-ce.htm (293 links) lists "Nubia", "Nueva Caceres", "Nueva Pamplona", "Nueva Segovia", "Nugent, Francis" (11150a), "Nugent, James", "Numbers, Use of, in the Church" (11151a), "Numismatics" (11152a) - no article on the book. Neither -ce page carries any exhaustiveness disclaimer. So the underlying negative is TRUE, but the registered evidence does not establish it and says so on its face. Corroborating checks I ran: 06413b.htm returns HTTP 404 (the row's "the article number between the last two being unassigned"); 11150a is "Francis Nugent", 11152a is "Numismatics", 11151b returns 404 - all three exactly as the Numbers row states.
column9: Register the pages that actually bear the negative - https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/g-ce.htm and /n-ce.htm - as the artifacts of edition.catholic-encyclopedia.alphabetical-index.newadvent-web-2026-08-27 (hash at fetch time), and cite those from the Genesis and Numbers gap rows; keep g.htm/n.htm only if their records are re-characterised. column8: I reopened the loader, which is the 'new evidence' the ledger rests on, and it says the opposite of the ledger on the decisive point. scripts/_chronology.py, immediately above the `needs a non-empty 'dates' list` raise, reads: 'Requiring a date of every event meant that withdrawing the only claim on a subject was impossible without deleting the subject, and where other claims anchor on it that cannot be done either. The corpus met this at `israel.monarchy.saul-accession` ... An event with no `dates` asserts nothing, returns nothing, and leaves the loci bound to it to whatever else reaches them - which is the honest answer when no ranked source has dated it. A composition unit still requires one'. The `raise` fires only on a `dates` key that is present and empty; an event with NO `dates` key is accepted, and `return ()` is the branch taken. The precedent is live at HEAD in the same file: events.yaml:3118 `israel.monarchy.saul-accession` carries no `dates` at all, and its own note says 'This event survives without a date because it is still a subject: two bindings name it and four claims are measured from it'. So the ledger's 'an event must carry a non-empty dates list, so dropping the claim would mean deleting the event and orphaning its bindings, losing verbatim Scripture testimony' is false three times over: the event may stand dateless, its one binding (bindings.yaml:2753) survives, and the verbatim Ezech. 24:18 words can live in the event `note`, where this corpus already puts verbatim testimony. The ledger's second support also fails on inspection. It says the stored shape 'is the same shape israel.judges.ark-comes-to-cariathiarim and israel.conquest.division-of-the-land already use correctly for an unquantified position.' I read both: ark-comes-to-cariathiarim has `parent: israel.judges.period` but `relative.of: israel.judges.ark-among-the-philistines`, and division-of-the-land has `relative.of: israel.conquest.war-against-the-kings-of-chanaan`. Both anchor on an ANTECEDENT event - a sequence - and in neither is the anchor the event's own container. The Ezechiel claim anchors on `israel.exile.ezechiel.ministry`, which is its own `parent`, i.e. the containing span; that is the very thing section 10.0 names, 'a duration may say what it sits within ... and `Date.anchor` deliberately does not return it. Containment is not offset.' Here `Date.anchor` (scripts/_chronology.py:396-402, `return self.relative.get('of')`) does return it. The claim's own note concedes it: 'Anchored to the ministry and to nothing narrower, because nothing narrower is stated.' What the ledger gets RIGHT, and I confirmed: nothing computes and nothing false is displayed - `tools/tpt scripture-chronology query Ezech.24.18 --json` shows the anchor is never emitted; the consumer sees only the label 'I spoke to the people in the morning, and my wife died in the evening', which is verbatim in the tracked Douay ('So I spoke to the people in the morning, and my wife died in the evening: and I did in the morning as he had commanded me'), and the refusal to borrow the Ezech. 24:1 dateline stands.
column9: Either (a) apply the audit's recommendation, which IS expressible: withdraw the single claim so the event carries no `dates` key, exactly as israel.monarchy.saul-accession does at HEAD, keep the containment where it already lives (`parent: israel.exile.ezechiel.ministry`), and move the verbatim Ezech. 24:16-18 morning/evening testimony and the Schets quotation into the event `note`, which already holds most of it (no gaps.yaml row is needed: Ezech.24.18 still returns `dated` from the inherited Ezech-scoped historical-setting and prophecy-given claims, as the live query shows); or (b) if the claim is to be kept, correct the ledger row, which currently states a loader constraint the loader does not impose and cites two precedents that anchor on antecedents rather than on containers. Re-dispositioning the row from `withdrawn-after-new-evidence` to `maintainer-disposition` with the true ground would at minimum stop the false statement about the loader from standing as the corpus's record of why this finding was dropped.
column10: The withdrawal reads the finding differently rather than defeating it. column3: the manifest does not surface a changed relative anchor as such
column8: Ten claims changed `date.relative.of` between 2330d63a5 and 214797e78. The manifest's `why` column names the change for seven of them only incidentally, and for three - israel.restoration.nehemias-tidings-of-jerusalem#0, israel.wilderness.mara-and-elim#0 and israel.wilderness.mary-stricken-at-haseroth#0 - says nothing but `changed:note`. The cause is in how the manifest was built: it compares `str(claim.date)`, and a `relative` date renders its `statement`, not its anchor, so an anchor moved without a restated statement is invisible. A wrong anchor is the class the cold audit rated `major` and the class §12 of these directions singles out, and a reviewer handed `changed:note` has no reason to open it.

column3: Howlett's 62-64 reconstruction of the Roman captivity, disputed. Finding S6-011 required the hedge on the begin endpoint to be carried; the lane extended the basis with the article's 'Perhaps we may say 62' sentence and added a note quoting Blass. In doing so it left the record with TWO `sources:` keys in one YAML mapping.
column5: Howlett, "Biblical Chronology", CE vol. 3 (1908), section "The apostles", retained text lines 227-229
column8: The source substance checks out verbatim. Retained line 229: 'Harnack places this event in 57, Lightfoot in 61, Ramsay in 60. Perhaps we may say 62, for he was sent to Rome by Festus, shortly after his arrival in Judea . But this was not long before the death of Pallas in A.D. 62 (Tac., Znn., XIV, lxv). In Rome St. Paul remained two years, hence till 64 ( Acts 28:30 ).' The new basis reproduces that sentence including the source's own space before the full stop after 'Judea', and the hedge 'Perhaps we may say' now stands on the begin endpoint as the finding required. Retained line 227 heads the section: 'Frederick Blass (Acta Apostolorum, p. 21) tells us of the chronology of the Acts of the Apostles that we cannot be certain of our dates within a less period than about ten years.' - so the note's quotation and its claim that the warning stands 'at its head' are both correct. THE DEFECT IS STRUCTURAL, NOT FACTUAL: src/sources/chronology/events.yaml line 1257 is `sources: [artifact.catholic-encyclopedia.volume-3.new-york-1908.newadvent-03731a-f5f96f04]` and line 1265, after the inserted `note:`, repeats the identical `sources:` line inside the same claim mapping. At 2330d63a5 the claim had one `sources:` line (old-events.yaml line 1250); the lane inserted a second while inserting the note and did not remove the original. A sweep of all four corpus YAML files finds this is the only duplicated key in the corpus.
column9: Delete one of the two identical `sources:` lines in event:apostolic-age.saint-paul-first-roman-captivity#1 - src/sources/chronology/events.yaml line 1265 is the redundant one, leaving the line 1257 occurrence between `basis` and `note`, which is the corpus's normal key order. No other change is needed on this row.
column10: Impact is confined to the file, which is why this is minor and not major: PyYAML's safe_load takes the last duplicate and both values are identical, so the loaded claim is correct, `tools/tpt scripture-chronology validate` still reports 'chronology corpus valid', and no consumer sees anything wrong. But duplicate mapping keys are invalid under YAML 1.2, a strict or round-tripping loader (ruamel with duplicate-key checking, yamllint) rejects the file, and the corpus is source data that must survive re-serialisation. The substance of S6-011 is correctly fixed; only this residue needs removing.

column3: Howlett's 'the monarchy was founded by Saul, 1020' withdrawn from catholic-traditional-v1, leaving the event with no claims at all and a new event-level note explaining the silence.
column5: Howlett, "Biblical Chronology", CE vol. 3 (1908), close of "The Exodus to the building of Solomon's Temple"; Driscoll, "Saul", CE vol. 13 (1912), whole article
column8: THE WITHDRAWAL ITSELF IS RIGHT, and the sources say so. Howlett's sentence, read in the retained text, closes a section built entirely on Egyptology and Assyriology (Ramses II 'reigned from 1348-1281 (Sayce)', 'we are driven to his immediate successor, Meneptah', Wellhausen and Stade treating 3 Kings 6:1 as a late insertion): "We conclude, therefore, that the date of the Exodus was about 1277, the monarchy was founded by Saul, 1020; David mounted the throne, 1002; Solomon in 962, and the Temple was begun, 958 B.C." The same article distinguishes that reckoning from tradition in its own voice - of the 1277 it says "This is not the traditional date of the Exodus", and later "We have fixed roughly the date of the revolt of the Ten Tribes for the year 936 B.C. But the traditional date is 975". So 1020 is a modern reconstruction, 4.3 excludes it, and as the subject's ONLY claim it was what the profile answered. The corpus is now consistent with itself: the 1277 from the same sentence is likewise recorded in israel.exodus.the-exodus's note and not held as a claim. The note's other premises check out: the CE "Saul" article (13486d) was read end to end and carries no date whatever - the only four-digit numbers in it are the 1912 copyright and 'Strasburg, 1674' in its bibliography. `query 1Kings.10.24` and `query 1Kings.11.15` now return `composition-only`, i.e. the book's composition chronology and no modern reconstruction, which is honest. DEFECT, in the note the withdrawal authored: it states that 'two bindings name it and four claims are measured from it'. Two bindings is right (narrated-event at 1Kings.10.17-27 + 11.14-15, utterance at 1Kings.12). FOUR IS NOW THREE. A grep of src/sources/chronology/*.yaml finds exactly three claims anchored on it - israel.monarchy.anointing-of-saul, israel.monarchy.deliverance-of-jabes-galaad, composition.book-of-judges#0. Four was true at 2330d63a5, where israel.judges.period#0 was the fourth; the correction lane's own re-anchoring (RR-024 / A2-029) removed it and this note was not updated to match. The identical stale count is repeated in scripts/_chronology.py::_claims, whose docstring says the corpus met this 'at `israel.monarchy.saul-accession`, whose single claim was a modern reconstruction 4.3 excludes and whose identity four other claims and two bindings depend on'. SECOND DEFECT: the model change the withdrawal depends on is in the loader only. guidance/scripture-chronology.md 6 still defines an event as 'an id, a title, an optional parent, and one or more dated claims', and nothing in the guidance admits a claimless event, so by the contract this review adjudicates by, the production corpus now holds an event the contract does not allow.
column9: Correct 'four claims are measured from it' to three in the note on israel.monarchy.saul-accession in src/sources/chronology/events.yaml, and correct the same count in the _claims docstring in scripts/_chronology.py ('four other claims and two bindings depend on'), or state it in a form that cannot go stale ('the claims that anchor on it, and two bindings'). Then amend guidance/scripture-chronology.md 6 so the contract admits what the loader now permits: an event is an id, a title, an optional parent and ZERO or more dated claims, with the ground the loader already gives - naming a subject is not the same act as dating it, and a subject other claims anchor on cannot be deleted to withdraw a claim. A composition unit must keep requiring one.
column10: The audit's E1-016 also asked for a gaps.yaml row so the subject reaches `undated-in-tradition`. Not authoring one was CORRECT and is not part of the finding above: _chronology.py consults gaps only where no assertion reaches the locus (`if assertions: return Answer(...)` precedes the gap loop), and 1 Kings 10-12 carry composition.first-book-of-kings, so a gap row there would be unreachable code. `composition-only` is the accurate status and 9.2's accounting still closes.

column3: Newly added on the call of Abram: the Septuagint total, label "1147", anchor israel.primeval.deluge, statement "1147 years from the flood to the call of Abraham, in the Septuagint", disposition alternate, with the note that carries the disposition rationale.
column5: Howlett, "Biblical Chronology", CE vol. 3 (1908), the Flood-to-Abraham table, final row, Septuagint column; and the same article's antediluvian table under "Creation to the flood"
column8: The date, anchor, attribution and both basis quotes are sound: "being respectively 367, 1017, and 1147" and the row label "Hence, number of years from Flood to Call of Abraham" are verbatim, and 1147 is the Septuagint column of that row. The defect is in the note, which was carried over unchanged from the withdrawn birth-of-Abram claim and now reads: "The spread between the Hebrew and the Septuagint here is seven hundred and eighty years, wider than the whole antediluvian disagreement, and no ranked source inspected for this corpus settles it." 1147 - 367 = 780 is right. The comparison is not. The same article's antediluvian section states "the total number of years in the Hebrew, Samaritan, and Septuagint differs, in the Hebrew, it being 1656, in the Samaritan, 1307, and in the Septuagint, 2242", and its table prints the row "Creation to Flood 1656 1307 2342". The WHOLE antediluvian disagreement is therefore 2242 - 1307 = 935 years by the narrative, or 2342 - 1307 = 1035 by the table - both wider than 780, not narrower. The corpus's own four deluge claims (1656 A.M., 1307, 2242, 2256) give 949 on the same computation. Only the Hebrew-to-Septuagint pair alone is narrower (586 by the narrative, 686 by the table), and the sentence says "whole", not "between the same two witnesses".
column9: In the note of event:israel.patriarchs.call-of-abram#3, either delete the clause "wider than the whole antediluvian disagreement", or restate it to the comparison that is true, e.g. "wider than the Hebrew-to-Septuagint spread of the same article's antediluvian table". Do not restate it as a comparison with the whole antediluvian spread, which is 935 years on the article's own narrative figures (1307 to 2242) and 1035 on its printed table row (1307 to 2342). The rest of the claim - date, anchor, statement, sources, disposition - is correct and needs no change.
column10: This is exactly the failure mode the brief names: prose that travelled with a relocated claim and was not re-read against the source. It reaches consumers - tools/tpt scripture-chronology query Gen.12.4 --json returns this note in full on the 1147 assertion. Severity minor: no date, event, attribution or source identity is falsified, and the second half of the sentence ("no ranked source inspected for this corpus settles it") and the disposition rationale after it are both sound.

column3: The ninth-century composition claim for Abdias re-disposed from `preferred` to `disputed`, and the note's stated ground for not authoring the section's two rival opinions replaced. Interval 900-801 B.C., label and basis unchanged.
column5: Gigot, "Abdias", Catholic Encyclopedia vol. 1 (New York, 1907), section "Date of the prophecy of Abdias", read in full
column8: Retained section read end to end. Opening: "there are various reasons, literary and exegetical , which prevents scholars from agreeing upon the date of its composition" -- verbatim in the note. First opinion: "Many among them (Keil, Orelli, Vigouroux, Trochon, Lesetre, etc.) assign its composition to about the reign of Joram (ninth century B.C.)." and "Hence it is inferred that the prophecy of Abdias originated between the reign of Joram and the time of Joel and Amos , that is, about the middle of the ninth century B.C." -- both verbatim in the basis, and every distancing verb the note lists is on the page: "we are told", "it is claimed", "Hence it is inferred", "The inference is said also to be confirmed". Second opinion: "Other scholars, among whom may be mentioned Meyrick, Jahn, Ackerman , Allioli , etc., refer the composition of the book to about the time of the Babylonian Captivity , some three centuries after King Joram." Third: "Others again, ascribe the present book of Abdias to a still later date" ... "connects necessarily the prophecy of Abdias with other works in Jewish literature [ Joel , Daniel , Zechariah 9-14 ] which, as they think, belong to a date long after the return from Babylon." Closing: "These, then are the three leading forms of opinion which prevail at the present day regarding the date of composition of the book of Abdias" -- the article settles none of them. Neither the second nor the third paragraph prints a year, so the note's "Neither prints a year" is true; the "(588-587 B.C.)" in the section belongs to the FIRST paragraph, on Nabuchodonosor.
column9: The disposition half of the correction is right and must stand. What must be finished is the note. As applied, the note now says of the second opinion that it "is not the modern critical voice SS4.3 excludes and could be authored", says of the third that it "is NOT authorable here" and gives two grounds for that, and then closes "Neither prints a year, but that is not why the second is left unauthored" -- so the corpus states in its own voice that an authorable, ranked-reported Catholic opinion is deliberately omitted and gives no ground for the omission. The false ground was removed and no true one was put in its place. Do one of two things: (a) author the second opinion as a second `disputed` claim on composition.book-of-abdias -- SS4.4 permits two disputed and no preferred, and a `relative` date carries exactly the shape the article states it in ({of, statement}, no magnitude), the ledger's own S5-007 row supplying a ready block anchored on israel.exile.seventy-years with statement "about the time of the Babylonian Captivity , some three centuries after King Joram"; or (b) replace the final sentence with the actual ground for leaving it unauthored. Do not leave the note asserting that a correct ground exists and withholding it.
column10: What the lane got right, verified independently: `disputed` is the correct disposition -- the article prints three leading opinions and decides none, which is SS4.4's definition exactly; a lone `disputed` is legal and loads (tools/tpt scripture-chronology query Abd.1.1 returns "composition | about the reign of Joram (ninth century B.C.) | disputed | inherited" and coverage.tsv still holds Abd.1.1-21 as composition-only, so no sibling or gap-row consequence was missed); the interval 900-801 B.C. is the ninth century B.C. correctly bounded and errs wider than the source's "about the middle", which the note discloses; the new note's claim that two of the five names are not Catholic authorities is correct (Keil and Orelli), and Gigot does cite Vigouroux, Trochon and Lesetre without edition identity. The defect is confined to the note's incomplete reasoning and the factual result is unchanged, hence minor. Note also that the audit's own action (S5-007) asked for both halves -- "Change the disposition to `disputed` ... and author the rival opinions the same section supplies rather than dropping them" -- and only the first half was done.

column3: The new alternate on 4 Kings: approximate-year 587 B.C., label "not long before, or shortly after, the fall of Jerusalem (587 B.C.)" - the figure demoted out of the preferred slot by RR-053, kept queryable with its conditionality on its face.
column5: the authorship paragraph
column8: The claim itself checks out. The article reads: "If Jeremias be indeed the author, it must be accepted as probable that he wrote the book not long before, or shortly after, the fall of Jerusalem (587 B.C. ); the last verses (xxv, 27-30) have possibly been added by a different hand." and, earlier, "Not a few among both older and more recent exegetes consider this probable." All three of the note's quotations are verbatim, including the source's space before the closing bracket in "(587 B.C. )". The note's factual reasoning is sound: 587 B.C. is earlier in time than the 562 the article ties its unconditional floor to, so the alternate does stand earlier than the article's own floor, and the year is Schets's own consequence rather than a third party's figure, which is why alternate rather than withdrawal is right. THE DEFECT IS STRUCTURAL. composition.yaml lines 1272-1273 carry `label:` TWICE inside this claim's `date:` block, identical text both times - the lane added a second copy of the line rather than replacing it. Confirmed by diff against 2330d63a5 (the second `label` is a `+` line) and by reading the file at HEAD. A duplicate-key-detecting loader over the corpus reports exactly three duplicate mapping keys, two of them the Kings labels: composition.yaml line 1214 (third-book-of-kings, RR-062's row), composition.yaml line 1274 (this row), events.yaml line 1265 (a duplicated `sources` on apostolic-age.saint-paul-first-roman-captivity, RR-004's row). `yaml.safe_load` - which scripts/_chronology.py uses - silently keeps the last, and both values are identical, so the consumer result is unchanged: query 4Kings.25.27 returns the correct label.
column9: Delete the duplicated `label:` line in composition.yaml (one of lines 1272/1273, inside composition.fourth-book-of-kings claim #1's `date:` block). Secondary, same row: the note asserts "SS4.3 and SS15.1(3) keep a figure standing inside a reported antecedent out of the profile's first answer". SS4.3 says no such thing - it names Ussher, modern critical chronology, and unsourced model recollection - and SS15.1(3) is about a figure the source REPORTS rather than asserts, which the note itself two sentences later concedes 587 is not ("the year is Schets's own consequence and not a third party's figure"). Either cite SS15.1(3) as an analogy and drop SS4.3, or restate the ground as what it actually is: an assertion made only inside a condition the article does not settle is not the article's unconditional answer.
column10: Reported as `minor` because the chronological result reaching a consumer is unaffected in both particulars. The duplicate key is nonetheless a defect the correction lane introduced into a source-of-truth file, and the loader will not catch it.

The article reads "If Jeremias be indeed the author, it must be accepted as probable that he wrote the book not long before, or shortly after, the fall of Jerusalem (587 B.C. )", and the note's supporting quotation "Not a few among both older and more recent exegetes consider this probable" and "the last verses (xxv, 27-30) have possibly been added by a different hand" are both on the page word for word; `precision: approximate-year` from {year: 587, era: bc} is the right shape for "not long before, or shortly after", and `query 3Kings.10.1 --json` renders it "about 587 B.C." as `alternate`. THE DEFECT IS STRUCTURAL, NOT FACTUAL. column3: The prophecy-given binding of Micheas 4-5 to the fall of Samaria is withdrawn and replaced by a lane comment recording the refusal and its stated ground.
column4: artifact.catholic-encyclopedia.volume-10.new-york-1911.newadvent-10278a-734c8637 (and the sibling retrieval -0de24478 the withdrawn row named)
column5: Van Hoonacker, "Book of Micheas", CE vol. 10 (1911): opening biographical paragraph and "Part two (chapters 4-5)"
column8: THE WITHDRAWAL ITSELF IS RIGHT. Reopened the article. The whole warrant of the deleted binding was a sentence about composition: "The difference of tone and contents clearly show that 4-5 must have been composed in other circumstances than 1-3. They probably date from shortly after the fall of Samaria in 722 B.C." Sec. 5 forbids reading a composition statement as another relation, and that sentence is already held with both hedges by composition.book-of-micheas.chapters-4-5, whose basis quotes it verbatim and whose note says "The hedge 'probably' is the article's own and is kept". Live effect confirmed: `query Mich.4.1` returns `Mich.4.1 composition-only` with one composition line, where the audit records it returning four disputed prophecy-given lines carrying the fall's own years. The refusal to re-relate as historical-setting is also grounded in the page: the occasion the article names is the withdrawal, not the fall - "the enemy left Palestine without attacking Jerusalem" and "Chapters 4-5 have preserved us an echo of the joy caused in Jerusalem by the removal of the danger" - both verbatim, and this corpus holds no event for it. fall-of-samaria is not orphaned: it keeps its narrated-event binding over 4Kings 17:1-6 and 18:9-12 (bindings.yaml:1266). THE DEFECT IS IN THE STATED GROUND. The replacement comment asserts that "the article says nothing about when the oracles were uttered, and remarks only that 'We do not, however, appear to possess any of his addresses prior to the reign of Ezechias.'" The article says more than that, in the sentence immediately before the one quoted: "Jerusalem was the scene of his ministry, and it occurred, as we learn from the title of his book, under the Kings Joathan (c. 740-735 B. column8: Retained article, the section's opening question: "Is this sole writer the Prophet Daniel who composed the work during the Exile (586-536 B.C.), or, on the contrary, some author, now unknown, who wrote this inspired book at a later date, which can still be made out?" -- so 586-536 is a parenthetical gloss on "the Exile" inside a question, exactly as the new note says. The article's own composition figure, further down the same paragraph: "Over against this time-honoured position which ascribes to Daniel the authorship of the book which bears his name, and admits 570-536 B.C. as its date of composition, stands a comparatively recent theory which has been widely accepted by contemporary scholars." The basis quotes this verbatim, along with "The traditional view, in vigour chiefly among Catholics , is to the effect that the whole work, as found in the Hebrew Bible, should be directly referred to Daniel, whose name it bears". The note's other quotations are all on the page verbatim: "It admits, indeed, that numerous alterations have been introduced into the primitive text of the book in the course of ages"; "in the time of Antiochus IV, Epiphanes (175-164 B.C.)"; and the article's verdict "Despite the fact that some of these arguments against the Danielic authorship have not yet been fully disproved, Catholic scholars generally abide by the traditional view, although they are not bound to it by any decision of the Church."

Its division into two books--at an awkward place, just in the middle of the history of Ochozias--did not exist in early times". column8: Read in the retained article, consecutively: "As to the date of its composition we possess no certain historical information. According to the general opinion, the Gospel is to be referred to the last decade of the first century, or to be still more precise, to 96 or one of the succeeding years." Both are verbatim, and the corrected basis is right on the point the old one got wrong: the admission is the IMMEDIATELY PRECEDING sentence, not the same sentence. The note's second route is also verbatim: the Monarchian Prologue "He [sc. the Apostle John] wrote this Gospel in the Province of Asia , after he had composed the Apocalypse on the Island of Patmos" and "This evidence would therefore refer the composition of the Gospel to A.D. 96 or one of the years immediately following." On the re-encoding: the source prints no "about" anywhere near 96 - I grepped for it - so SS10's approximate-year ("one point, the source's own 'about'") did not fit, and "96 or one of the succeeding years" is by construction a window, which is SS10's `interval` ("the subject falls somewhere within from..to"). The upper bound 100 is the close of "the last decade of the first century", the wider statement the sentence's "or to be still more precise" is refining, and the note says so on its face. That reading is consistent with the corpus's own no-year-zero rule (SS10.1), which puts the first century at 1-100, and with the sibling Durand claim on the same unit running to 100. I verified the rendering change reaching a consumer: query John.3.16 --json now returns "date": "96 A.D. to 100 A.D." where an approximate-year renders "about 124 B.C." (checked against the 2Mach epitome claim) - so the note's statement about the old "about 96 A.D." display is accurate. SS4.4 unaffected: both claims on this unit are `disputed`, none preferred.

column3: New unit over 2Mach 1:1-10, the first prefixed letter, with a single preferred claim: precision `year`, 124 B.C., label "dated in the year 188 of the Seleucid era (i.e. 124 B.C.)".
column5: section "Contents", the sentence bounding the two letters; section "Author and date"
column8: The article, verbatim: "The book proper (ii, 20-xv, 40) is preceded by two letters of the Jews of Jerusalem to their Egyptian coreligionists (i, 1-ii, 19). The first (i, 1-10a), dated in the year 188 of the Seleucid era (i.e. 124 B.C.), beyond expressions of goodwill and an allusion to a former letter, contains nothing but an invitation to the Jews of Egypt to celebrate the feast of the Dedication of the Temple". `year` and not `approximate-year` is right: the article says "dated in", with no hedge, and both the Seleucid year and its B.C. equivalent are the source's own, as the note says. The scope boundary was checked in the tracked Douay, not assumed: 2Mach.1.10 reads "In the year one hundred and eighty-eight, the people that is at Jerusalem, and in Judea, and the senate, and Judas, to Aristobolus, the preceptor of king Ptolemee, who is of the stock of the anointed priests, and to the Jews that are in Egypt, health and welfare." - so Bechtel's i,10a/10b division does fall inside one Douay verse exactly as the unit note says, 10a being the date-line and 10b the second letter's salutation. I then tested the note's load-behaviour claim rather than taking it: I copied the corpus to scratch, widened the second letter to 1:10-2:19 so the two units overlap on 1:10, and loaded it. It LOADS - _refuse_ambiguous_inheritance keys a verse-range span on (system, book, chapter, first) only, so two equal-width ranges with different start verses are never compared - and chronology('2Mach.1.10') then returns the first letter's 124 B.C., the earlier-authored unit, because the query-time tie-break at _chronology.py:1810 is a strict `unit.width() > best.width()`. The note's statement that such a verse "is settled by authoring order, not by the narrowest-wins rule, because Unit.width() ranks whole-book, whole-chapter and verse-range and not verse counts" is therefore exactly true of this loader (Unit.width returns 0/1/2), and the non-overlapping scopes are a deliberate avoidance of a silent tie, not a redundant one. Live: 2Mach.1.1 and 2Mach.1.10 both answer with this unit, `direct`.
column10: The consequence is that 2Mach.1.10, most of whose text is the second letter's salutation, is answered with the first letter's 124 B.C. Either assignment mis-answers part of a verse that the source itself splits; the lane took the half that prints the date grounding the claim and disclosed the choice in the unit note, which is the right way to make it. Note that composition.yaml's own file header states more strongly that "two units of equal width over one verse is a load error" - my experiment shows that guarantee holds only where the two ranges share a start verse. That header line is unchanged since 2330d63a5 and is not this lane's doing.

The section "Time of his ministry" reads: "According to the title of the book, Osee prophesied during the reign of Jeroboam II in Israel , and in the time of Ozias , Joatham, Achaz , and Ezechias , kings of Juda, hence from about 750 to 725 B.C. None of the historical allusions with which the prophecy is filled appears to be connected with any event later than the reign of Manahem ( circa 745-735)... Every string the binding note and the event's two claims quote is verbatim, including the source's own hedge 'about' and its printing of 750-735 without era letters. The re-typing is the correct one: the verb is 'Osee prophesied' and the heading is 'Time of his ministry', which is when the oracles were uttered - Sec. 5's `prophecy-given` - and NOT when the book was written, which the article never treats. I verified that absence rather than assuming it: the remaining sections, 'The book of Osee' (contents, the marriage question, Van Hoonacker's division), 'Style and text' (Jerome on the style, the integrity of the text, alleged interpolations) and 'Teaching', carry no date of writing and no per-oracle date - the closest the article comes is undated ('it would appear that the dynasty of Jehu still occupied the throne', 'No doubt Menahem was already reigning'), so the note's 'dates no oracle of the book separately' holds. Live: `query Os.4.1` returns `prophecy-given | about 750-735 | preferred | inherited` and `prophecy-given | from about 750 to 725 B.C. | alternate | inherited`, and no composition line; `python` over composition.yaml confirms no unit's scope names Os, and the withdrawn unit's place carries a lane comment pointing at the event. column10: No gaps.yaml row is needed and one would have been wrong: gaps.yaml's own header says a status is what a locus reaches when nothing dated reaches it, and `prophecy-given` is substantive, so every verse of Osee is `dated`; authoring undated-in-tradition over the same loci would give them two statuses. column3: The cold audit's one critical finding. The Catholic Encyclopedia's Flood-to-Abraham totals 367 / 1017 / 1147 were carried on the BIRTH of Abram and overstated every one by seventy-five years; the correction moves all three to the CALL, re-dispositions them alternate beneath Genesis 12:4, and leaves the birth holding only the 720-year claim.
column5: Biblical Chronology, CE vol. 3 (1908), the Flood-to-Abraham table and the paragraph following it (retained text lines 135-163); Genesis 12:4, tracked Douay-Rheims
column8: All nine required checks were made from the source and from production, and all nine hold. (1) THE TABLE ROW. Read in the retained text of 03731a, the table's rows run: "Years from birth of Sem to birth of Abraham" 392 / 1042 / 1172; "Deduct years of Sem's age at time of flood" 100 / 100 / 100; an unlabelled result 292 / 942 / 1072; "Add for age of Abraham at time of his call" 75 / 75 / 75; "Hence, number of years from Flood to Call of Abraham" 367 / 1017 / 1147. The narrative below it reads "the numbers in the table above differ in the Hebrew, Samaritan , and Septuagint , being respectively 367, 1017, and 1147". The label says Call, and the arithmetic that reaches it adds the seventy-five. (2) SEVENTY-FIVE AT THE CALL. .scratch/cold-audit/verse.py Gen.12.4, tracked Douay: "So Abram went out as the Lord had commanded him, and Lot went with him: Abram was seventy-five years old when he went forth from Haran." That is the preferred rank-1 claim's exact statement, quoted verbatim in its basis. (3) THE OLD ANCHOR IS GONE. At 2330d63a5 israel.patriarchs.birth-of-abram carried four claims, three of them the 367/1017/1147 relative-to-deluge figures, all `disputed`, with a note conceding "the terminus is recorded here as stated in the heading and the ambiguity is not resolved". At HEAD it carries exactly one claim, the 720-year relative to the Exodus. (4) NO DUPLICATE STALE COPIES. grep for 367, 1017 and 1147 across the whole of src/sources/chronology/*.yaml returns hits only inside the call-of-abram block and inside the birth-of-abram note that records the history; nowhere else in the corpus. (5) THREE DISTINCT ALTERNATIVES SURVIVE. All three are present on call-of-abram as separate claims, each naming its text-family: "367 years from the flood to the call of Abraham, in the Hebrew", "1017 ... in the Samaritan", "1147 ... in the Septuagint". (6) SOURCE AND PROVENANCE. Each names 03731a and nothing else; the quoted grounds - "as a rule, the Greek and Samaritan agree against the Hebrew", "being respectively 367, 1017, and 1147", "must be greatly augmented, in order to allow time for such a development of civilization" - are all verbatim in the retained text, and the Ussher-free rank-6 attribution is right. The 720 claim's grounds on the birth are likewise verbatim: "These figures, added, give 290; add to this 430 (the number of years spent by Israel in Egypt) and we get 720 years, which would be the length of time between the birth of Abraham and the Exodus" and "215 years being required for the sojourn in Canaan , as we have to subtract 75, the age of Abraham when he came to Canaan , from 290". (7) RANK AND DISPOSITION. On call-of-abram: one `preferred`, Genesis 12:4, rank 1; three `alternate`, all rank 6; no `disputed`. SS4.4 satisfied on rank alone, since rank 1 is strictly higher than every alternate's rank 6. On birth-of-abram: a lone `disputed`, which SS4.4 permits. (8) BINDINGS RESOLVE TO THE CALL. `query Gen.12.4 --json` returns all four call-of-abram claims at scope Gen.12.1-5 and nothing anchored to the Flood on the birth; `query Gen.11.26 --json` returns only the 720-year birth-of-abram claim at scope Gen.11.26-27. The intervals reach the call verse and no longer reach the birth verse. The anchor arithmetic that settles it is real in the corpus: israel.primeval.deluge holds A.M. 1656 (events.yaml:1981, from the "Deluge" article's "the Masoretic text assigns it to the year 1656 after the creation"), so 1656+292 is the birth and 1656+367 the call, as the note says. (9) THE REGRESSION TEST GENUINELY FAILS. I copied the corpus to a scratch directory, mutated only the copy, monkeypatched _chronology.CORPUS_ROOT and ran tools/tests/test_chronology.py::TrackedHardCaseTests::test_a_source_interval_lands_on_the_endpoint_the_source_names against each. Control (unmutated copy): OK. Mutation A, the pre-correction state restored verbatim from git show 2330d63a5 (three claims back on birth-of-abram, call-of-abram left with only Genesis 12:4): FAILED at line 1410, "Items in the second set but not the first: '367 years from the flood to the call of Abraham, in the Hebrew' / '1017 ...' / '1147 ...'". Mutation B, the three claims duplicated back onto birth-of-abram while call-of-abram keeps them: FAILED at line 1417, assertEqual(flood_intervals("israel.patriarchs.birth-of-abram"), set()) - "Items in the first set but not the second" listing all three. So both limbs of the guard bite, on both shapes the defect could take. src/ was never touched; `git status --short src/` is empty.
column10: The correction also does what SS10.2 asks in the harder direction: it does not collapse birth and call into one event to make the arithmetic tidy, and the test asserts that Genesis 12:4 still anchors the call on the birth. The birth-of-abram note keeps the unlabelled 292/942/1072 row on the record as something the table reaches but does not state as a claim, which is the right refusal. The three alternates are `relative` and therefore carry no magnitude, so nothing computed off the old anchor - which is why, as SS10.2 says, the error read perfectly.
